summary: Provides the common definitions for the structure and identification of management information for TCP/IP-based internets, working with companion memos for the MIB and the network management protocol. It was replaced by RFC 1155.

eli5.summary: Before you can measure things on a network, you need agreed ways to name and describe each measurement. This memo gives that naming scheme.

questions: what is the structure of management information
how are snmp objects named and organized
what is the internet object identifier tree
subtitle: The grammar and naming scheme for network management objects

tldr.problem: Network devices need a standard way to name and describe the things that can be monitored, without defining the monitoring protocol itself.
tldr.mechanism: Defines an object identifier hierarchy, data types using ASN.1, and rules for how managed objects are named and described. Separates naming concerns from protocol concerns.
tldr.outcome: Allows many different network management protocols to use the same object definitions. Replaced by RFC 1155 with minor changes.

today: RFC 1155 replaced this with minor improvements in 1990.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Network management requires defining what can be monitored and controlled on each device, separate from defining how to fetch and set those values. This specification describes the Structure of Management Information (SMI), the naming scheme and data definitions that management protocols use.

The SMI focuses on organizational concerns: how to assign names to management objects and what data types they can have. It explicitly does not define the actual management objects (that is the job of the Management Information Base), nor does it define the protocols used to access them (such as SNMP). This separation allows the naming scheme to be reused by many different management protocols.
sections.eli5: This sets the naming rules and describes what types of data (like numbers or text) can be measured. The actual measurements and how to get them are defined elsewhere.

sections.title: Object Naming and Hierarchy
sections.content:
All management objects are named using an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, a hierarchical sequence of integers that traverses a global tree. The root is unlabeled, with three children administered by ISO, the CCITT, and a joint body. The Internet subtree, administered by the Internet Activities Board, starts with the prefix 1.3.6.1.

Under the Internet node are four major subtrees: directory (reserved for future use), mgmt (for IAB-approved objects), experimental (for testing), and private (for vendor-specific extensions). The private.enterprises subtree allows vendors to register their products and define objects for them without central coordination.

Each object type has both an OBJECT IDENTIFIER (the numeric name like 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0) and an OBJECT DESCRIPTOR (a human-readable name like sysDescr). This pairing lets both machines and humans refer to the same object.
sections.eli5: Objects get numbered addresses organized in a tree, like a filing system. For example 1.3.6.1.2 is for official management objects, and 1.3.6.1.4.1 is for company-specific things.

sections.title: Data Types and Syntax
sections.content:
The SMI uses Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1) to define object types, but restricts the full generality of ASN.1 for simplicity. Permitted primitive types are INTEGER, OCTET STRING (for byte sequences), OBJECT IDENTIFIER, and NULL.

Objects can also be constructed using SEQUENCE (for ordered lists of mixed types) and SEQUENCE OF (for tables of identical entries). Constructor types allow aggregation: a device can report a list of interfaces, for example, where each interface is a sequence containing speed, status, and other attributes.

The SMI also defines application-wide types used in management: Counter (a non-negative integer that wraps at 2^32-1), Gauge (an integer that can increase or decrease), TimeTicks (hundredths of a second since an epoch), and IpAddress (a 32-bit IP address).
sections.eli5: Objects can be simple numbers or text, or they can group multiple related things together, like how a table has rows and columns.

sections.title: Defining Managed Objects
sections.content:
Each object definition includes five fields: an OBJECT DESCRIPTOR and OBJECT IDENTIFIER for the name, the abstract syntax (data type), the semantics (a description of what the object means), the access level (read-only, read-write, write-only, or not-accessible), and the status (mandatory, optional, or obsolete).

Implementations must ensure their objects have consistent meaning across multi-vendor environments. An object type is a template; an object instance is a specific value at a specific time. A network manager queries instances, not types.

The SMI provides macros like OBJECT-TYPE that allow MIB documents to formally define objects. For example, the MIB might define an object type sysUpTime (how long the system has been running) with SYNTAX TimeTicks, ACCESS read-only, and STATUS mandatory.
sections.eli5: To define something you want to measure, you give it a number, a name, a data type, and say whether it's readable, writable, or both.

sections.title: Extending and Versioning
sections.content:
The SMI rules ensure that management software can support multiple versions of the MIB simultaneously. New versions of the Internet-standard MIB can declare old object types obsolete (without deleting them), add new object types to an existing list, or define entirely new objects.

However, new versions cannot change the semantics of an already-defined object without changing its name. This guarantees that code written for version 1 will understand version 2 objects with the same names.
sections.eli5: When the rules change, old objects stay in place so old software keeps working. New things can be added, but existing things cannot change meaning.

references.text: Thomson, S. and K. McCloghrie, "Management Information Base for network management of TCP/IP-based internets", RFC 1066, August 1988.
